title: Who killed the first transatlantic cable?
subject: sciences
description: In August 1858, a cable joined Europe and America for the first time, and Queen Victoria congratulated President Buchanan. Three weeks later the line was dead: the story of an electrician in too much of a hurry and a cable that was built wrong.
author: guido-manuel-de-la-torre-olvera

hero.hook: The cable that united two continents was already dying when the world celebrated it.

blocks.text: On **August 16, 1858**, a telegraph cable carried a message from [[Valentia Island]] in Ireland to Trinity Bay in Newfoundland: congratulations from Queen Victoria to the American president, James Buchanan. Two continents were joined for the first time. Three weeks later, the line fell silent. The blame landed on [[Wildman Whitehouse]], the company's electrician, who had been driving enormous voltages into the wire to force the signals through.

He was not innocent. But the historian **Donard de Cogan**, examining cable recovered from the seabed, found manufacturing defects in it: in places, the copper core sat off-center inside its insulation. Whitehouse did not kill a sound cable. He finished off a damaged one, and the damage was there before it sailed.

sections.title: The first message crosses the ocean

blocks.text: The first message across the ocean was not the Queen's. On the same day, the directors of the [[Atlantic Telegraph Company]], the company laying the cable, wrote from Britain to their American counterparts: "**Europe and America are united by telegraph**..." And the message went on.

blocks.caption: New York celebrates the cable in September 1858: the crowd on Broadway, photographed by William England.

blocks.text: In the exchange that followed, President Buchanan replied to the Queen. He called the cable a triumph more glorious, because far more useful to mankind, than any ever won by a conqueror on a battlefield, and he hoped it would prove a bond of **perpetual peace** between the two nations. Nobody sending these words knew that the cable carrying them was already dying.

sections.title: Two theories, and the cheaper one wins

blocks.text: The men building the cable did not agree on how it would work. The physicist [[William Thomson]] predicted that signals would crawl through a long submarine cable, an effect he called [[retardation]]. Whitehouse, who had **no training in physics**, disputed it. Given overnight access to long underground telegraph lines, he joined them end to end until they matched the Atlantic distance, sent signals through, and declared there would be no problem.

Thomson answered that a buried cable and an underwater cable do not behave the same way. He also tested copper of supposedly identical specification: its electrical resistance varied by a **factor of two**. A thin core was not only slow, it was unpredictable. A thicker one was needed. But manufacture was already under way. The thinner, cheaper cable won.

On **August 5, 1858**, the cable reached Valentia and Thomson handed over to Whitehouse. Throughout the voyage, Thomson had been reading the faint incoming pulses on his [[mirror galvanometer]], an instrument sensitive enough to catch a signal that had crossed an ocean.

Whitehouse disconnected it and attached his own, far cruder equipment. Nothing registered. So he drove up to **2,000 volts** into the cable to force a response, pushing insulation that was already defective past its limits. The Queen's message reached Newfoundland, but Whitehouse could not read the confirmation coming back.

He waited until **August 17** to announce it. What he did not announce: he had reconnected Thomson's galvanometer to read the message, then retyped it into his own printing telegraph, so that the paper tape would look as though it came from **his instrument**.

sections.title: The proof in a bucket of seawater

blocks.text: In **September 1858**, the line died for good. Whitehouse was dismissed; Thomson took over at Valentia to work out what had happened. The board tested offcuts of the same cable in seawater. Sound samples took **thousands of volts** without complaint. A sample pierced by a single pinhole burned a wide hole through its insulation. Voltage alone was survivable. Voltage through a manufacturing fault was not.

blocks.caption: "The Atlantic Telegraph", an illustrated chart by G. W. Bacon, c. 1865: route map, the Great Eastern, cable cross-sections.

blocks.text: The worst of it lay close to home: the first hundred miles out of Ireland were leftover **1857** cable, spliced in, with its copper core sitting off-center. Before it died, the line carried **732 messages**. In 1865, the [[Great Eastern]] tried again and lost the cable in mid-ocean. In 1866, it succeeded.
One of the 732 messages countermanded an order for two regiments in Canada to sail for England: a single dispatch saved the government 50,000 pounds.

events.title: The cable comes ashore
events.detail: At Valentia, Thomson hands over to Whitehouse.

events.title: Another failure
events.detail: The Great Eastern loses the cable in mid-ocean.

events.title: Success
events.detail: The Great Eastern finally links the two shores.

blocks.text: Whitehouse's 2,000 volts did not kill a sound cable but finished off a badly made one: Thomson's physics had been right, and the cheaper version had won.
